prompt.brief: Design a change-risk service that analyzes proposed code, configuration, and infrastructure changes against service topology and incident history, then recommends guarded rollout plans and windows.
successSignals: Define change identity, diff/config features, service ownership/topology, historical incident labels, risk explanations, and model versions.
Score blast radius and collision risk without blocking all delivery; distinguish evidence-backed risk from uncertainty and recommend canaries/approvals.
Separate CI/CD admission from asynchronous feature building and incident correlation; make scores reproducible and idempotent.
Explain feedback loops, concept drift, sensitive code, overrides, rollback, auditability, observability, and rule-based fallback.

functional: Ingest proposed changes and context, compute affected services/features, score risk, explain drivers, and recommend rollout gates or windows.
Integrate with CI/CD and change management, record deployment outcomes/incidents, support approvals, overrides, canary progression, and rollback.
Version features/models, protect source data, replay historical changes, delete sensitive evidence, and survive unavailable topology or model services.
nonFunctional: Return a preliminary risk score within 30 seconds and never bypass mandatory policy gates when the ML service is unavailable.
Score 100k changes per day across thousands of services without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 100k changes/day across 10k services and 1M historical incidents
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Change-risk service commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Change-risk service writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Change-risk service version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Change-risk service by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Change-risk service work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Change-risk service projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Change-risk service projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Change-risk service records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Change-risk service latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
